ARTICLE 1 — PROJECT DESCRIPTION AND SCOPE

1.1 What we're building. The Provider is building a Revenue Data Mart for the Client — a curated set of Snowflake tables and dbt models that consolidates the Client's revenue, billing, and usage data into a single source of truth that the Client's analytics team and finance team can query directly. The goal is to replace the Client's current pile of Looker SQL extracts and Google Sheets pivots with a versioned, tested, documented dbt project that the Client owns and can extend.

1.2 What's in scope. The Provider will:

(a) Audit the Client's source systems (Stripe, Salesforce, the Client's internal usage logs, the Client's HubSpot CRM) and document the source-to-target field mappings.

(b) Build the dbt staging layer that lands raw data from each source into staging models.

(c) Build the dbt mart layer that produces the four core revenue mart tables: customers, contracts, billing_events, and usage_events.

(d) Build dbt tests for each model (uniqueness, not-null, referential integrity, accepted-values).

(e) Build dbt documentation for each model and column.

(f) Wire up the dbt project to run nightly via the Client's existing Airflow scheduler.

(g) Provide read-only access patterns and example queries for the Client's analytics team.

(h) Conduct a 60-minute walkthrough with the Client's analytics team and a 60-minute walkthrough with the Client's finance team.

1.3 What's out of scope. The following are not included. Any of these, if requested, requires a Change Order under Article 8:

(a) Source-system data quality remediation. The Provider builds models against the Client's source data as it exists. If the source data has gaps, errors, or inconsistencies, the Provider documents them but does not remediate them at the source.

(b) Looker, Tableau, or any BI tool work. The Provider produces curated tables; downstream BI tool work is the Client's responsibility.

(c) Real-time or near-real-time pipelines. This project produces a nightly batch pipeline only.

(d) Any data sources beyond the four named in Section 1.2(a). Adding sources requires a Change Order.

(e) Any data marts beyond the Revenue Data Mart. Marketing, product, or finance marts beyond revenue are out of scope.

(f) Snowflake account setup, warehouse sizing, or cost optimization. The Provider assumes the Client has a working Snowflake account.

(g) Airflow setup or DAG authoring beyond wiring up dbt to run on the existing schedule.

(h) Data governance or data catalog work beyond the dbt-built documentation.

(i) Any work involving personally identifiable information beyond the standard email and customer-name handling already in the source systems. The Provider does not perform PII discovery or PII masking.

1.4 Engagement period. The Provider will perform the In-Scope Activities from the Project Start Date through the Project End Date set out in Article 3.

(a) The Client's Snowflake account is operational and provisioned with sufficient warehouse capacity for the dbt build and test runs. The Provider's models will use a dedicated warehouse named in Schedule A.

1.1 Project Objectives. The State Agency has engaged the Contractor to modernize the State Agency's permit application portal — the public-facing web application through which residents and small businesses apply for and renew permits administered by the State Agency. The objectives are to (a) replace the legacy mainframe-backed application portal with a cloud-native web application, (b) improve accessibility to comply with the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.1 Level AA, (c) reduce average application completion time, (d) provide bilingual support (English and Spanish), and (e) preserve all data continuity and audit-trail requirements applicable to the State Agency under state records laws.

(a) Conduct a Discovery and Current-State Assessment, including stakeholder interviews, legacy system documentation review, and review of the State Agency's data classification policy.

(b) Produce a Target State Architecture Document and a Migration Plan.

(c) Build the new application portal as a cloud-native web application using the technology stack approved by the State Agency's Office of Information Technology Services (Schedule A).

(d) Migrate the historical permit data from the legacy mainframe system to the new application portal's data store, with full data validation and reconciliation.

(e) Implement the bilingual interface (English and Spanish) for all public-facing pages.

(f) Implement WCAG 2.1 Level AA compliance, with third-party accessibility audit and remediation.

(g) Implement role-based access controls for State Agency employees and integrate with the State Agency's enterprise single sign-on system.

(h) Implement audit trails and records retention controls compliant with the State Agency's records retention schedule.

(i) Conduct user acceptance testing in coordination with the State Agency's UAT team.

(j) Conduct end-user training for State Agency employees and produce written training materials.

(k) Provide a 90-calendar-day post-launch hypercare period.

(a) Modifications to the State Agency's enterprise single sign-on system. The Contractor integrates with the existing system as is.

(b) Modifications to the State Agency's existing payment processing infrastructure. Permit fees are processed through the State Agency's existing payment infrastructure.

(c) New permit programs or new permit types not currently supported by the legacy system.

(d) Modifications to the State Agency's enterprise data warehouse beyond delivering data extracts in the State Agency's standard format.

(e) Modifications to the State Agency's internal case management systems.

(f) Any work product subject to U.S. export-control restrictions.

(g) Translation services into languages other than Spanish.

(h) Print fulfillment, mail handling, or any non-digital services.

1.2 In-Scope Activities. Subject to the Assumptions set forth in Article 6, the Provider shall perform the following activities (the "In-Scope Activities"):

(a) Discovery Phase. Conduct a structured discovery of the Client's existing Oracle 12c environment, including a catalog of databases, schemas, tables, views, stored procedures, materialized views, scheduled jobs, triggers, and ETL pipelines feeding the environment. The Discovery Phase shall produce a written Discovery Report (a Deliverable under Article 2).

(b) Target Architecture Design. Design the target Snowflake architecture, including warehouses, databases, schemas, role-based access control, network policies, masking policies, data sharing configurations, and resource monitors. (c) Schema Conversion. (d) ETL Pipeline Rebuild. Rebuild the existing Informatica PowerCenter ETL pipelines as Snowpipe-based ingestion pipelines or as Snowflake tasks-and-streams, depending on the source system characteristics for each pipeline.

(e) Data Migration and Validation. (f) Cutover and Hypercare. Coordinate with the Client to schedule and execute the production cutover for each migrated workload, and provide hypercare support for thirty (30) calendar days following cutover, including incident triage, root-cause analysis, and remediation of any data integrity issues directly attributable to the migration.

(g) Knowledge Transfer. Conduct knowledge transfer sessions for the Client's data engineering team and produce written runbooks documenting the migrated environment, the validation procedures, and the rollback procedures.

(f) Any work product subject to export-control restrictions under the International Traffic in Arms Regulations (ITAR) or the Export Administration Regulations (EAR).

ARTICLE 1 — PROJECT DESCRIPTION AND SCOPE

1.1 Project Objectives. The Client has engaged the Provider to conduct (a) an external penetration test of the Client's internet-facing assets, (b) an internal penetration test of the Client's corporate network, and (c) a web application penetration test of the Client's customer-facing application, for the purpose of identifying exploitable vulnerabilities and producing a written report that the Client may use for SOC 2 Type II evidence and for regulatory and customer security questionnaires.

1.2 Testing Scope and Targets. The In-Scope Activities are limited to the testing targets identified in Schedule A (the "In-Scope Targets") as follows:

(a) External Penetration Test. The In-Scope Targets are limited to the Client's internet-facing IP ranges and DNS names listed in Schedule A-1, totaling no more than two hundred fifty-six (256) IPv4 addresses and the Client's primary corporate domain.

(b) Internal Penetration Test. The In-Scope Targets are limited to the Client's corporate network segments listed in Schedule A-2, conducted from a Provider-supplied test endpoint connected to the Client's network at a single physical location to be agreed by the Parties.

(c) Web Application Penetration Test. The In-Scope Target is the Client's customer-facing web application accessible at the production URL listed in Schedule A-3, tested in a dedicated non-production environment provisioned by the Client.

1.3 Testing Methodology. The Provider shall conduct testing in accordance with (a) the OWASP Testing Guide v4 for the web application portion, (b) the Penetration Testing Execution Standard (PTES) for the network portions, and (c) the Provider's own internal methodology documented in Schedule B.

1.4 Out-of-Scope Activities and Targets. The following are expressly out-of-scope. Any of the following, if requested, requires a Change Order under Article 8:

(a) Any target not explicitly listed in Schedule A. The Provider shall not test any IP, hostname, application, or system that is not explicitly listed in Schedule A.

(b) Denial-of-service testing. The Provider shall not perform any test that is designed to cause, or that the Provider has reason to believe is likely to cause, an interruption of service to any production system.

(c) Social engineering, phishing campaigns, or physical security testing. Those services are out-of-scope and shall not be performed under this SOW.

(d) Testing of any system that is not owned or operated by the Client. The Provider shall not test any third-party system, even if such system is reachable from an In-Scope Target.

(e) Remediation services or hands-on assistance with the Client's remediation of identified findings. The Provider's role is to identify and report; remediation is the Client's responsibility.

(f) Any retest of remediated findings beyond the single retest included in Section 2.1(d) of this SOW.

1.5 Rules of Engagement. The Provider shall conduct testing in accordance with the following rules of engagement:

(a) Testing shall be conducted only during the testing windows agreed in writing by the Parties and recorded in the testing kickoff document.

(b) The Provider shall use only test traffic source IP addresses pre-approved by the Client and listed in the testing kickoff document. The Client shall whitelist these source IPs as appropriate.

(c) The Provider shall maintain a real-time activity log identifying each test action and the time of execution. The Provider shall make the activity log available to the Client on request.

(d) Upon discovery of any critical-severity finding (as defined in Section 1.6) that creates an active exposure of customer data or that materially threatens the availability of any production system, the Provider shall within two (2) hours notify the Client's designated security contact by telephone and follow up in writing within four (4) additional hours.

(e) The Provider shall not exfiltrate, copy, store, or retain any production customer data encountered during testing other than the minimum amount necessary to demonstrate the existence of a vulnerability in the final report. Such demonstration data shall be hashed, redacted, or otherwise sanitized in the report.

(f) The Provider shall halt any testing activity immediately upon written request by the Client's designated security contact.

1.6 Severity Definitions. Findings shall be rated using the following severity scale:

(a) Critical — exploitable vulnerability that grants the attacker unauthenticated access to customer data, administrative access to a production system, or remote code execution on a production system.

(b) High — exploitable vulnerability that grants the attacker authenticated access beyond the user's privilege level, or that could be combined with a moderate degree of additional effort to achieve a Critical-severity outcome.

(c) Medium — exploitable vulnerability with limited direct impact, or vulnerability that requires user interaction or authenticated access to exploit.

(d) Low — vulnerability with minimal direct impact, primarily a hardening or defense-in-depth concern.

(e) Informational — observation that does not represent an exploitable vulnerability but that the Provider believes is relevant to the Client's security posture.
